strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: combining test-time scaling (soft best-of-n) with speculative decoding to approximate the KL-regularized optimal policy efficiently is a sensible and timely direction.

The paper provides actual theoretical guarantees, unlike the closely related RSD baseline (Liao et al., 2025): a KL bound between the induced distribution and the tilted target policy (Theorem 1) and a reward-gap bound for the full algorithm with rejection (Theorem 2), with proofs given in the appendix.

The core rewriting of the tilted distribution as a reward-likelihood-tilted distribution over the small model is simple and elegant, and the coverage assumption (chi-square divergence between base and small model) is a reasonable and interpretable condition.

Experiments include a meaningful set of baselines (RSD, S-BoN with small and big model), report wall-clock inference time and acceptance rates (Table 2), and the empirical convergence of GSI to S-BoN(big) as n grows is consistent with the theory (Figure 2).
The paper is generally well-written, with a clear algorithm description and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., GSI being slower than RSD, gap to S-BoN(big) shrinking with n).
weaknesses: Limited empirical scope: only one model pair (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B) with a math-specific PRM, evaluated only on math reasoning benchmarks. No evidence the method generalizes to other domains (e.g., safety alignment, code, open-ended generation) or other model families/sizes.

Evaluation reliability concerns: results are averaged over only two random seeds, with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several reported differences (e.g., GSI 51.3 vs. S-BoN(big) 54.0 mean accuracy at n=64) are sizable in the opposite direction, so the claim that GSI 'in certain settings even outperforms soft best-of-n with π_B' is overstated relative to the aggregate evidence.

The theoretical bounds are loose and somewhat incremental: Theorem 1's bound depends exponentially on e^{β‖r‖∞} and the chi-square divergence, and both proofs lean heavily on Lemma 1 from Verdun et al. (2025). The paper does not empirically validate the bound's tightness or the coverage constant C_∞, and the distributional guarantee does not actually apply to the full algorithm π_GSI (only the reward-gap result).

Missing ablations and sensitivity analysis: β=20 and threshold u=0.5 are 'selected empirically' but no sweep or ablation over β, u, or n (per-model) is reported; the authors explicitly defer sensitivity analysis and separate n for small/big models to future work, yet these directly affect the accuracy–speed trade-off that is the paper's selling point.

Practicality concerns are underexplored: the method requires hosting three models (small, big, PRM) on separate H100s, and computing log π_B for tilt/rejection means a big-model forward pass is still needed whenever the tilt falls below threshold; a per-step cost breakdown versus S-BoN(big) and RSD beyond the aggregate seconds/step in Table 2 would strengthen the efficiency claims.
Reproducibility is weakened: the code availability 'link' in the abstract and Appendix A is empty, so the stated code release cannot be verified.

Novelty is moderate: the method is a natural composition of known components (importance-tilted soft best-of-n, standard speculative-decoding accept/reject intuition, and a threshold-triggered fallback to the big model), and the main technical contribution is the analysis rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: combining reward-guided test-time scaling with speculative decoding to reduce inference cost is a relevant and timely direction.

The paper provides actual theoretical guarantees (Theorem 1 on KL convergence to the KL-regularized optimal policy, Theorem 2 on the reward gap vanishing with n), which distinguishes it from prior heuristic approaches such as RSD (Liao et al., 2025).
The core identity rewriting the tilted distribution as a re-weighting of the small model's samples is simple and elegant, and the proof of Theorem 1 is correct and self-contained.

Experiments include an inference-time analysis (Table 2) with acceptance rates, which is the right metric for a speculative-decoding-style method, and show a real speed-accuracy trade-off: GSI is faster than S-BoN with the big model while achieving comparable accuracy.
Code availability and use of standard benchmarks (MATH500, OlympiadBench, Minerva Math) with publicly available models and PRM aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited empirical scope: evaluation uses a single model pair (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B), a single PRM, and only mathematical reasoning tasks. Results are averaged over only two random seeds, with no variance estimates or statistical significance tests, despite many gaps between methods being small (e.g., 51.1 vs 49.0 mean accuracy).

The headline claim that GSI 'even outperforms soft best-of-n with the base model' is overstated. In Table 1, S-BoN (big) achieves higher mean accuracy (52.6/54.0) than GSI (51.1/51.3) on every dataset except MATH500 at n=16. GSI's advantage is essentially only computational (0.88 vs 1.14 s/step), which should be framed honestly as a speed-accuracy trade-off rather than an accuracy improvement.

The theoretical guarantees rest on a very strong coverage assumption (C_inf(x) < infinity, Eq. 3), which is unrealistic for autoregressive LLMs and never verified or even empirically probed. Moreover, the required sample complexity grows like e^{2 beta ||r||_inf} chi^2 / epsilon, so the bounds are extremely loose and provide no practical guidance on choosing n.

Theory does not cover the actual algorithm: Theorem 1 applies only to the reward-likelihood tilted S-BoN without the rejection step, while the deployed GSI (Algorithm 1, with threshold u) only receives a reward-gap bound. The rejection step, which empirically matters most (Figure 2), is thus analytically uncharacterized.

Key hyperparameters (u = 0.5, beta = 20) are 'selected empirically' with no sensitivity analysis reported, and the acceptance-rate vs. accuracy trade-off motivating them is not shown. RSD's threshold is taken from its paper, raising fairness concerns about baseline tuning.

Missing baselines from the broader test-time scaling literature: no comparison to self-consistency, PRM-guided tree/beam search, or other reward-weighted sampling variants, which are the natural competitors for step-level reward-guided decoding with a PRM.

The technical novelty is incremental: the algorithm is essentially soft best-of-n over speculative samples with a reward threshold, and the main KL bound is a direct corollary of Lemma 1 from Verdun et al. (2025); the paper's contribution over RSD is primarily adding likelihood tilting and a theoretical analysis.

The claim that GSI 'converges to S-BoN on pi_B as n increases, which empirically confirms Theorem 1' is not a meaningful confirmation: convergence by construction is expected, and the bound's constants are never empirically instantiated.
Presentation issues: Figure 2 is small and hard to read, key axis labels overlap, and the discussion of why GSI(w/o rej) lags at small n is deferred to vague future work.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated algorithmic contribution: GSI elegantly combines soft best-of-n sampling, speculative sampling from a small model, and reward–likelihood tilting, with a rejection-sampling fallback to the base model.

The paper provides genuine theoretical guarantees (Theorem 1: KL bound to the optimal tilted policy; Theorem 2: expected reward gap vanishing in n), which distinguishes it from RSD (Liao et al., 2025), which lacks distributional fidelity guarantees.
The proof of Theorem 1 is correct and self-contained (building on Lemma 1 of Verdun et al., 2025), and the coverage assumption (3) is stated explicitly.

Experiments cover three standard math reasoning benchmarks with reasonable baselines (RSD, S-BoN with small and big models), and the paper reports inference time and acceptance rates, not just accuracy.
Code availability and a clear vLLM-based implementation improve reproducibility.
The empirical finding that GSI outperforms RSD and S-BoN(small) while being faster than S-BoN(big) supports the practical relevance of the method.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 is a fairly direct application of the existing Lemma 1 from Verdun et al. (2025) to a re-parameterized reward, and Theorem 2 follows from standard Cauchy–Schwarz arguments. The main theoretical bound contains the factor e^{2β||r||∞}; with β=20 and rewards in [0,1], this factor is e^40, making the bound essentially vacuous in the experimental regime. The paper does not discuss this gap between theory and practice.

The empirical advantage over the target method (S-BoN with π_B) is weak or negative: mean accuracy is 51.1/51.3 for GSI vs. 52.6/54.0 for S-BoN(big), and GSI only wins on MATH500. The abstract's claim that GSI 'in certain settings even outperforms soft best-of-n with π_B' oversells results that are, on average, worse than the target distribution it approximates.

Very narrow evaluation: a single model pair (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B), a single PRM, and only math reasoning tasks. No non-math domains (e.g., safety alignment, instruction following) despite the method being generic. Results may not generalize, especially since the coverage assumption is plausibly violated for weakly related model pairs.
Statistical rigor is limited: only two random seeds, no standard deviations or significance tests reported, and several gaps (e.g., GSI vs. S-BoN(big) on OlympiadBench) are within plausible noise.

Missing ablations: the hyperparameters u=0.5 and β=20 are 'selected empirically' but no sensitivity analysis is provided; the contribution of the rejection step is shown only via one figure, and the interaction between u, β, and acceptance rate is not systematically studied.

A mismatch between theory and algorithm: the rejection/threshold step (lines 8–13 of Algorithm 1) is not covered by Theorem 1, and Theorem 2 applies only to the golden reward, not to the induced policy distribution. The actually deployed algorithm π_GSI therefore lacks the paper's central policy-fidelity guarantee.

Practical deployment cost is understated: the method requires three models (small, big, PRM) each on its own H100, and per-step cost (0.88s at n=16) is only modestly below S-BoN(big) (1.14s), while being slower than RSD (0.77s). The speed–accuracy trade-off story would benefit from a Pareto-style analysis across compute budgets.

The chi-square divergence in the required sample complexity (Theorem 1) between a 1.5B and 7B model is likely enormous, so the promised convergence to π_{β,B} may require n far beyond the tested range (n ≤ 256); Figure 2 shows convergence toward S-BoN(big) but this could be coincidental rather than a confirmation of Theorem 1 as claimed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated algorithm: the reformulation of the tilted policy as a distribution over the draft model with likelihood-corrected (tilted) rewards r~ = r + (1/β)log(πB/πS) is simple, elegant, and practically effective for combining soft best-of-n alignment with speculative-style sampling.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 provides a clean KL guarantee between the tilted distribution and the proposal distribution under a standard coverage assumption, requiring none of the asymptotic or randomized-threshold assumptions needed by the concurrent SPECS bound. Theorem 2 additionally bounds the expected golden-reward gap at O(1/√n).

Comprehensive evaluation: five reasoning benchmarks, three random seeds with 95% CIs, comparison against RSD (reimplemented with matched hyperparameters), S-BoN with both draft and target models, plus an ablation-rich appendix (β, threshold u, acceptance rates, runtime, Pareto frontier of u vs. n).

Honest and informative latency analysis (Table 2/3): the paper shows GSI trades a slightly higher per-step cost than RSD for much higher accuracy, and analyzes why RSD's near-100% acceptance rate causes it to collapse to S-BoN(small).

Qualitative analysis of reasoning traces illustrates both the benefit (rejecting wrong draft steps with high raw reward but low tilted reward) and the failure mode (rejecting correct but differently-worded draft steps) of the log-ratio term.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in isolation: the method is a fairly direct composition of soft best-of-n (Verdun et al., 2025) with speculative decoding ideas, and is very close to concurrent work (RSD, SPECS). The main differentiators are the tilted-reward correction and the unconditional KL bound, which strengthens but does not fundamentally redefine the line of work.

The bound in Theorem 1 is essentially vacuous at practical settings: with β = 20 and rewards in [0,1], the required sample size scales as (χ²+1)e^{2β‖r‖∞} ≈ χ²·e^40, astronomically larger than the n ≤ 256 used in experiments. The paper never discusses this looseness or connects theory to practice, which weakens the claimed theory-practice bridge.

Theorem 2 relies on Assumption 2, which is strong and unnatural (average golden reward on Y≥ exceeding the global average under πn_β,B, and πn_β,B(Y≥) ≥ π̃GSI(Y≥)); these conditions are neither verified nor plausibly checkable, so the reward guarantee is largely conditional.

The distributional guarantee applies only to π̃GSI (without the rejection step), whereas the deployed algorithm includes rejection and resampling; the interaction of rejection with the KL guarantee is not analyzed.

Overclaiming: the abstract and discussion state GSI 'sometimes even outperforms soft best-of-n with πB', but Table 1 shows S-BoN(base) beats GSI in average accuracy at every n (e.g., 61.3 vs 59.5 at n=4; 62.5 vs 60.7 at n=256); on aggregate GSI approaches but does not surpass the base-model S-BoN. The empirical verification of Theorem 1 claimed in Sec. 5.1 is also indirect.

Narrow empirical scope: a single draft/target model pair (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B), a single PRM, and math-only tasks; no evaluation of generalization across model families, model gaps, or non-reasoning domains. Comparison to SPECS uses reported numbers on different sample sizes (N=100 vs N=500), which the authors acknowledge is not directly comparable.
Reproducibility is undermined by a missing code URL ('The code is available at:' is blank in both the abstract and reproducibility section).

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core algorithmic idea—rewriting the tilted policy πβ,B as an exponentially tilted version of the draft model using the reward-likelihood correction r̃ = r + (1/β)log(πB/πS)—is elegant and gives a clean way to combine soft best-of-n with speculative decoding.

Theoretical contribution is real: Theorem 1 provides a KL bound to the tilted distribution without requiring assumptions on n or the threshold being random (contrasting with concurrent SPECS), and the proof in Appendix A is short, correct-looking, and self-contained.

Empirical evaluation covers five reasoning benchmarks with confidence intervals over three seeds, and includes useful ablations over β and the acceptance threshold u, acceptance-rate analysis versus RSD, and runtime comparisons.
The analysis of RSD's near-100% acceptance rate (collapsing to soft BoN with the small model) is an insightful empirical finding about a competitor method.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a fairly direct combination of soft best-of-n (Verdun et al., 2025) with the log-likelihood correction from speculative decoding applied to reward-guided sampling; the space of closely related methods (RSD, SPECS, speculative rejection) is crowded and the delta over them is modest.

The main theoretical result beyond Theorem 1 (Theorem 2) relies on Assumption 2, which is strong and essentially directionally assumes the conclusion (that the tilted BoN distribution has higher average golden reward on the accept set and is more likely to produce high-tilted-reward samples); these assumptions are neither verified nor verifiable in practice, so the 'expected reward guarantee' is weaker than advertised.

The distributional guarantee in Theorem 1 is per reasoning step, but the algorithm iterates over T steps; KL divergence (and reward gaps) would accumulate over steps, and the paper does not discuss the full-sequence guarantee, which is the quantity that actually matters for end-to-end accuracy.

Evaluation scope is narrow: a single model pair (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B) from the same family and only math/STEM reasoning tasks. Generalization to other domains, model families, or draft-target gaps is untested.

GSI never actually surpasses the natural upper baseline S-BoN(base) on average (e.g., 60.7 vs 62.5 at n=256), and on MMLU-STEM it is substantially worse (50.7 vs 57.3). The abstract's framing that it 'even outperforms soft best-of-n with πB' relies on cherry-picked dataset/scale settings.

No direct experimental comparison with SPECS (concurrent and highly related work); the comparison is made using numbers reported on different (100 vs 500 sample) subsets, which the authors themselves admit is not directly comparable.

The latency claims are partially undermined by the fact that computing the tilted reward requires a forward pass of πB for every draft sample to obtain log πB(y|x), so the target model is still invoked every step; the speedup over S-BoN(base) (Table 2/3) is modest (~35-40%).
Reproducibility is compromised: the code repository link is empty ('The code is available at:'), so the stated code availability cannot be verified.

The rejection threshold u and β=20 are tuned empirically, while RSD's threshold is fixed to its paper's value; hyperparameter tuning asymmetry could favor GSI, and the authors note the optimal u depends on n (left as future work), suggesting the reported results are not the method's best operating point in a principled sense.

Discussion of failure modes is anecdotal (Figures 3, 8): GSI rejects correct draft steps when πB words them differently, indicating the tilted reward can be misleading—this limitation is acknowledged but not quantified.

strengths: Clear and simple core idea: the exact change-of-measure identity rewriting the tilted policy πβ,B as a distribution over the draft model with tilted rewards r̃ = r + (1/β)log(πB/πS) is elegant, and the resulting algorithm is easy to implement and understand.

The theory is sound as written: the proof of Theorem 1 (KL bound via Lemma 1 of Verdun et al. and Jensen's inequality) is correct and self-contained, and Theorem 2 gives an explicit O(1/√n) expected-reward bound. The distributional guarantee is stronger than the expected-reward-only guarantee of RSD and does not require the asymptotic approximations needed by SPECS.

Consistent empirical gains over the closest baseline (RSD) and S-BoN with the draft model across five reasoning benchmarks, with confidence intervals over three seeds; the ablation studies over β and u, acceptance-rate analysis, runtime tables, and qualitative reasoning traces are thorough and honest (including failure cases where GSI rejects correct steps).
Honest and well-positioned related work, including a fair discussion of concurrent SPECS and its differing assumptions; runtime analysis candidly notes GSI is slower than RSD.
Good discussion of why the tilted reward (vs. raw reward) matters, illustrated concretely in Appendix B.5 (e.g., a step with r=0.998 receiving tilted reward 0.148).
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantees are practically vacuous at the sample sizes used. Theorem 1 requires n ≥ ((χ²+1)e^{2β||r||∞} − 1)/(e^ε − 1); with β=20 and ||r||∞=1 (the experimental setting), this is astronomically large even for χ²=0 and ε=1 (~10^18). The paper does not acknowledge or quantify this theory–practice gap.

Theorem 1 applies only to the rejection-free variant π̃GSI; the full GSI algorithm (with the acceptance threshold, which drives most of the empirical gains per Figure 2) has no distributional guarantee. Theorem 2 additionally requires Assumption 2, which partially assumes the desired conclusion (higher average golden reward on the accepted region) and involves the unknown golden reward r*.

Empirical scope is narrow: a single model pair (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B), a single PRM, and math reasoning only. Generalization to other domains, draft/target ratios, and weaker coverage regimes (where the coverage assumption likely fails) is untested.

The comparison to SPECS is not methodologically sound: accuracies are taken from their paper on N=100-sample subsets vs. this paper's N=500, so the claimed '+11.5% on MATH500' is not a controlled comparison.

The distributional target πβ,B is arguably better approximated by S-BoN with the base model: S-BoN(b) outperforms GSI on average at n=64 and n=256 (62.4/62.5 vs 60.7), while GSI's speed advantage over S-BoN(b) shrinks to nearly nothing at n=256 (5.80 vs 5.88 s/step). Since computing log πB for each draft sample requires a target-model forward pass anyway, the practical speedup is modest (~1.3x at n=4), which weakens the 'efficient' framing.
Errors compound across reasoning steps: the guarantees are per-step, with no analysis of the multi-step composition over T iterations.
The code availability statement in both the abstract and the reproducibility section contains an empty URL ('The code is available at:'), undermining reproducibility claims as submitted.
Results are sensitive to the threshold u, which is tuned empirically; the authors themselves note an n-dependent schedule would be better, leaving a key hyperparameter effectively hand-tuned.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated algorithm: GSI cleanly combines soft best-of-n test-time scaling with speculative sampling by rewriting the tilted distribution π_{β,B} as an exponential tilt of the draft model with tilted rewards r̃ = r + (1/β) log(π_B/π_S), which is an elegant observation enabling efficient reward-guided decoding.

First speculative test-time scaling method with an explicit distributional guarantee to the optimal tilted policy (Theorem 1), and a proof of convergence of expected (golden) reward at rate O(1/√n) (Theorem 2); the proofs in Appendix A appear technically sound and rely appropriately on prior soft-BoN analysis (Verdun et al., 2025).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five reasoning benchmarks, two model families (Qwen2.5-Math, Qwen3) with different draft/target size ratios, n up to 256, 95% CIs over three seeds, latency measurements (Tables 1, 5, 6), acceptance-rate analysis, ablations over β and u, empirical χ² divergence estimates to check the coverage assumption, and qualitative reasoning traces comparing GSI vs RSD.

Honest and transparent reporting: the paper acknowledges GSI is slower per step than RSD and S-BoN(small), that Assumption 2 is an idealization (Remark 3), that the Theorem 1 bound is not tight for practical hyperparameter choice, and analyzes failure cases (e.g., tilted rewards rejecting correct steps).
Careful positioning against closely related concurrent work (SPECS, RSD) with clear articulation of the theoretical differences (e.g., no assumption that block size → ∞, unlike SPECS).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are largely vacuous in practice: with β = 20 and r ∈ [0,1], the bound in Theorem 1 requires n on the order of e^{2β‖r‖∞} = e^40 times the χ² divergence, i.e., astronomically large n; the authors concede the bound is not useful for practical guidance, so the 'provably approximates the optimal policy' claim is only asymptotically meaningful.

Theorem 2 relies on Assumption 2, which is strong and essentially unverifiable (it assumes π^n_{β,B} has higher average golden reward on Y≥ than on all of Y and dominates the acceptance probability of π̃_GSI); Remark 3 partially mitigates this but the finite-n bound depends on these assumptions.

The headline claim that GSI 'in certain settings even outperforms soft best-of-n with π_B' is overstated: in Tables 2 and 3, S-BoN (base) achieves higher average accuracy than GSI in essentially every (model, n) configuration; GSI's real advantage is the latency-accuracy trade-off, which the abstract and discussion frame less clearly.

The comparison to SPECS is indirect and potentially unfair: it uses numbers reported in their paper on N=100-sample subsets vs. the authors' N=500-sample subsets, and the claimed 'up to 11.5% improved accuracy' is derived from non-comparable evaluations; no direct head-to-head experiment is possible due to missing code, weakening this part of the empirical story.
Reproducibility statement is incomplete: the 'Reproducibility' section says code is 'available at' with no URL, so reproducibility cannot be verified at submission time.

Hyperparameters (β = 20, u = 0.5) were selected on MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math; while the authors claim out-of-the-box transfer, the ablations show sensitivity (sharp phase transition in acceptance ratio between β = 8 and β = 20, and optimal u varying with n), suggesting brittleness that a threshold schedule only partially addresses.

Limited scope of evaluation: only Qwen-family models and math/STEM reasoning tasks; all results depend on a single PRM (Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B), and the PRM itself consumes a large fraction of runtime (Figure 4), so gains may not generalize to other domains or weaker/noisier reward models.

GSI offers only a modest accuracy gain over RSD (+1.3 to +6 points average) at the cost of lower throughput per step (e.g., 2.33 vs 2.94 steps/s at n=4), so the practical significance of the improvement over the strongest simple baseline is not always clear-cut.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the algorithm (Algorithm 1) is simple, well-motivated, and easy to follow; the rewriting of the tilted distribution as a distribution over the draft model with tilted rewards is a clean observation.

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: five reasoning benchmarks, two model families (Qwen2.5-Math, Qwen3), multiple values of n, latency measurements with runtime breakdowns (Table 1, Figs. 4-6), and ablations over beta and the acceptance threshold u.
The paper reports confidence intervals over seeds, provides implementation details, and includes a reproducibility statement with a code repository and reasoning trace examples.
The latency measurements are honest: the authors acknowledge that GSI is slower than RSD and S-BoN(small) and that the PRM dominates runtime, rather than only reporting favorable numbers.
The discussion of related work, including concurrent work (SPECS, RSD), is thorough and fair in positioning the differences.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are practically vacuous. Theorem 1 requires n >= ((chi^2 + 1) e^{2 beta ||r||_inf} - 1)/(e^epsilon - 1); with the beta = 20 used in all experiments and rewards in [0,1], this is on the order of e^40, astronomically beyond any practical n. The authors themselves admit in Appendix C.5 that the bound should not be used for practical guidance, which substantially undercuts the headline claim of 'provably approximates the optimal tilted policy'. Moreover, the worked example in Appendix C.5 silently switches to beta = 1, inconsistent with the experimental setting.

Theorem 2 relies on Assumption 2, a strong and entirely unverified assumption (that S-BoN on the target model has higher average golden reward on the high-tilted-reward set, and that its mass there exceeds the draft-policy's mass). No empirical evidence is provided that this assumption holds, so the O(1/sqrt(n)) expected-reward guarantee is not well supported.

The main empirical contribution is weaker than the framing suggests. Across Tables 2 and 3, GSI is consistently below S-BoN with the base model on average accuracy at every n (e.g., Qwen2.5 averages 54.4 vs 58.2 at n=1; 60.7 vs 62.4 at n=64). The abstract's claim of 'in certain settings even outperforming' S-BoN(base) is cherry-picking from per-dataset cells within confidence intervals. The value proposition reduces to: much worse accuracy than S-BoN(base), slightly better than RSD, at somewhat lower latency.

The comparison to SPECS, the closest concurrent method, is not conducted: it relies on cross-paper numbers on different (and differently sized) random subsets (N=100 vs N=500), which the authors themselves note 'might not be directly comparable'. This is a significant gap given the paper explicitly positions itself against SPECS in the introduction and related work.

The theoretical contribution has limited novelty in isolation: the proof of Theorem 1 is a direct application of Lemma 1 from Verdun et al. (2025) with importance-tilted rewards, plus a chi-square bound; the additional rejection-threshold step, which is what actually drives the empirical gains, is not covered by any guarantee.

The gain over RSD, the primary baseline, is modest (roughly 1-3 accuracy points on average) and comes at a latency cost (GSI is slower per step than RSD in all settings in Table 1), making the practical significance of the improvement debatable.

Several hyperparameters (beta = 20, u = 0.5) are selected on MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math and the claimed out-of-the-box transfer is asserted rather than demonstrated through a systematic cross-dataset sensitivity study; the beta ablation shows a sharp phase transition between beta=8 and beta=20, suggesting brittleness of the choice.

The KL guarantee in Theorem 1 is stated for the no-rejection variant (tilde-pi_GSI), i.e., precisely the variant that performs worse empirically, while the full method pi_GSI (which is what is evaluated) is excluded from the guarantee. The paper's actual algorithm therefore has no distributional guarantee attached to it.

strengths: Clear and elegant core idea: rewriting the tilted (KL-regularized) policy π_β,B as a tilt over the draft model π_S using reward-likelihood corrected rewards r̃ = r + (1/β) log(π_B/π_S), enabling reward-guided speculative test-time scaling with distributional guarantees.

Meaningful theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 gives an explicit, assumption-minimal KL bound to the optimal tilted policy (with a concrete sample-complexity condition), improving over RSD (which has only a weak expected-reward guarantee) and SPECS (whose bound requires asymptotic/idealized assumptions). Theorem 2 gives an O(1/√n) expected golden-reward guarantee.
Proofs in the appendix appear correct and are built carefully on prior results (Verdun et al. Lemma 1), including a formal version of Theorem 2 with an explicit bound.

Extensive empirical evaluation: five reasoning benchmarks, two model families across different sizes (1.5B/7B and 1.7B/14B), three random seeds with 95% CIs, latency/throughput tables, runtime breakdowns, and ablations over β and the acceptance threshold u.

Honest and transparent reporting: the paper does not overclaim—GSI consistently beats RSD and S-BoN with the draft model, and only approaches (rather than uniformly beats) S-BoN with the base model; the rejection step's contribution is disentangled; practical caveats about the theoretical bound and timing reliability are acknowledged.

Nice qualitative analysis (reasoning traces showing tilted rewards catching errors the raw PRM reward misses, e.g., the rounding example), plus empirical estimation of the chi-squared divergence appearing in the theory.
The setting is timely (efficient test-time scaling / reward-guided decoding) and the method is well-positioned against the closest concurrent work (RSD, SPECS).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the algorithm is essentially soft best-of-n over draft samples with likelihood-corrected rewards plus a rejection threshold. The main technical ingredients (tilted distributions, S-BoN approximation) are inherited from prior work (Korbak et al., Verdun et al., Beirami et al.), and the algorithmic delta relative to RSD/SPECS is a correction term and threshold choice.

Theory–practice gap: the sample-complexity bound in Theorem 1 is vacuous at the operating point actually used (β=20, r∈[0,1] gives a factor e^{40} in the required n); the authors themselves concede the bound is not practical guidance. Theorem 2 relies on Assumption 2, whose second part (π^n_{β,B}(Y_≥) ≥ π̃_GSI(Y_≥)) is strong and not verifiable at deployment time.

Empirical gains are mixed and modest: GSI is slower than RSD and S-BoN(small) at all settings; it does not beat S-BoN(base) on average at any n (Table 2 shows 60.7 vs 62.5 at n=256 for Qwen2.5-Math); the headline 'reduces latency by up to 28%' is a best-case comparison against S-BoN(base), and end-to-end latency is dominated by the 7B PRM (Figure 4), so a smaller PRM would be needed for the gains to matter.

The claim that GSI 'sometimes even outperforms soft best-of-n with the target model' is based on individual datasets/CIs and does not hold on average; the title/abstract framing slightly overstates this.
Comparison to SPECS is indirect (using numbers reported on N=100-sample subsets vs. the paper's N=500), so the claimed superiority over SPECS is not established under controlled conditions.

Latency evaluation has caveats acknowledged by the authors (models on separate GPUs, vLLM batching idiosyncrasies, no parallelization of PRM verification and log-likelihood computation), and some runtimes in Table 6 (e.g., S-BoN(s) 0.2 s/step at n=1 matching the Qwen2.5 numbers, S-BoN(b) missing a CI) suggest possible inconsistencies.
Reproducibility statement is incomplete (code URL is blank in the submitted PDF), and there are several typos/truncated sentences (e.g., 'Our implementation is available a') that should be fixed.
